drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Here's your opener. A health insurer runs a claims assistant for its adjusters. Policy says
drills.answer_line: SAM: And A is the tempting distractor. It's better than nothing
drills.stem: Policy says adjusters may only see claims from their own region. Claude refused every red-team prompt, but in production an adjuster politely asks for another region's claim and gets it. Which change closes the gap?

options.A: Add the regional rule to the system prompt
options.B: Deterministic authorization check in the retrieval tool, keyed to server-injected adjuster identity
options.C: Output classifier that flags claim numbers from other regions
options.D: Move to a larger model with stronger safety training

drills.why: A system prompt steers but does not enforce. A deterministic check on server-injected identity removes the risk at its root: the forbidden record never reaches the context.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A retail support agent answers from a product knowledge base
drills.scenario: Retail support agent issuing store credit
drills.stem: A retail support agent answers from a product knowledge base and can issue store credit through a tool. Today the only control is a toxicity judge on the final response. Which two additions most directly close the largest gaps?

options.A: Deterministic authorization on caller identity and credit limit before the store-credit tool runs
options.B: Screen retrieved knowledge-base passages for embedded instructions before they enter the context
options.C: System prompt sentence: never issue credit above $50
options.D: A second toxicity judge from a different vendor on the output
options.E: Weekly sampled review of credit transactions

drills.why: A puts a provable gate in front of the only side effect. B covers indirect injection, the dominant vector the design ignores. C is a probabilistic fix for a deterministic need.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A field-service agent schedules technician visits, which customers
drills.answer_line: ALEX: B. Stakes drive routing, confidence sets the volume.
drills.stem: A field-service agent schedules visits customers can rebook freely, and orders non-returnable parts above $5,000. Reviewers handle about 40 items a day; the agent makes 2,000 decisions. Which routing design fits?

options.A: Route every decision below 90% confidence to review
options.B: Low-confidence part orders to pre-action approval, sample scheduling, show inputs, output and flag reason
options.C: Route by confidence alone, threshold set low enough to fit 40 items
options.D: Post-action audit of all part orders

drills.why: Stakes drive routing, confidence sets the volume. A ignores stakes, C sets the threshold by queue size, D catches the bad order after the money is spent.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A bank's credit-support assistant is challenged by a regulator
drills.answer_line: SAM: Yes. A outsources a problem that entered through the bank's own corpus.
drills.stem: A regulator asks a bank whether similar applicants were treated comparably by its credit-support assistant. The team logs final recommendations only. What is the most important change?

options.A: Ask the model vendor for its latest bias evaluation
options.B: Log inputs, retrieved context, output and routing per decision, queryable and retained per the register
options.C: System prompt instruction to treat all applicants equally

drills.why: Only B lets anyone reconstruct a decision or rule out a source. A outsources a corpus problem, C is an instruction without evidence, D hides subgroup harm.

drills.question_line: SAM: Before the recap, your turn. Pause and name the five task statements from today
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Guardrails and safety controls, risks and failure modes, human in the loop
drills.prompt: Name the five task statements from today, and the giveaway in a stem that points to each one.
drills.answer: Guardrails, risks and failure modes, human in the loop, compliance, bias and fairness. Giveaways: side-effect tool, poisoned document, reviewer capacity, named regulation, one group doing worse.
